analysis.one_liner: Bars Congress from delegating lawmaking power to federal agencies, voiding rules not fully written by Congress.
analysis.headline: Sen. Rand Paul's bill to strip federal agencies of lawmaking power drew no cosponsors and died in the Homeland Security Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal law to prohibit any Act of Congress from delegating legislative power — to the President, agencies, courts, states, or anyone else. Any law, rule, presidential directive, or regulation that wasn't "fully and completely" written by Congress itself would have no force, and anyone affected could sue to block its enforcement. Six months after passage, the Comptroller General would have to report to Congress every existing statute that contains such a delegation. In practice, because most modern statutes set broad goals and leave the details to agencies, this would invalidate enormous amounts of federal law and regulation.
analysis.who_benefits: Under the bill's own theory, the public gains because only elected legislators could make binding rules, restoring the accountability the Constitution assigns to Congress. In practical terms, the people and entities best positioned to use it are regulated businesses and individuals facing federal enforcement, who could sue to have any rule not fully spelled out in statute thrown out. Heavily regulated industries stand to gain the most, since most of the rules binding them are agency-issued under broad statutory grants.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any Act of Congress from delegating legislative power to the executive branch, agencies, courts, states, or any other entity, and voids any law or rule that violates the ban [S2][S3].

Gives any person aggrieved by an executive branch action under a noncompliant law the right to sue the United States for relief, including an injunction against enforcement, with de novo review [S2][S3].
Requires the Comptroller General to report to Congress within six months identifying every pre-existing statute that contains a prohibited delegation of legislative power [S2][S3].
Preserves narrow exceptions: presidential proclamations, internal agency operating rules, and conditions on grants or contracts are not treated as delegations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who relies on federal rules written by agencies under broad statutory mandates. Because statutes like the clean air, food safety, drug approval, financial, and labor laws delegate technical detail to agencies, those rules would lose force under the bill's 90-day trigger, leaving consumers, workers, and patients without the specific protections — while Congress would have to write every technical standard itself, a task it has never been able to perform at that scale.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, workers, and patients relying on federal rules

drawbacks.text: The bill would deny force to most existing statutes and regulations, because Congress historically writes broad mandates and leaves the specifics to agencies; the enforcement clause and 90-day effective date would strip those rules with no transition period [S2][S3].

Agencies could no longer issue or change any rule that regulates private conduct unless authorized by an Act of Congress that fully complies with the ban, effectively ending federal rulemaking as it currently works and creating a vacuum in areas like drug safety, financial markets, and environmental standards [S2][S3].

Even the Comptroller General report requirement acknowledges the scale of the problem the bill creates: it asks for an inventory of every statute containing a delegation so they can be 'phased out,' implying most of the federal code is noncompliant [S2][S3].

The strongest argument for the bill — that unelected officials currently make binding law — is real, but courts have long allowed delegation under a lenient standard, and no similar proposal had advanced in Congress, suggesting no workable alternative scheme was on the table.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The constitutional concern the bill raises — that agencies combine rule-writing, enforcement, and adjudication — is a genuine long-running debate. But this bill addresses it by invalidating, all at once, the specific rules that implement nearly every major federal law, with no replacement process and only narrow exceptions. Whatever accountability gains its sponsor intended would come at the cost of an immediate, sweeping voiding of consumer, worker, health, safety, and financial rules. On balance, the cure as drafted would have caused far more disruption than the accountability problem it was meant to fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced S. 1575, the 'Write the Laws Act,' in the Senate on June 15, 2015 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill, which never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: federal agencies kept their existing rulemaking authority and the body of regulations built under delegated power stayed fully in force, so the regulatory system and the interests that operate within it were preserved by default.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and the existing regulatory system

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Write the Laws Act and referred it to committee; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor facing no recorded opposition in either direction.

industries.industry: Heavily regulated industries (finance, pharmaceuticals, energy, food, workplace safety)
industries.note: If enacted, most rules these industries operate under — issued by agencies under broad statutory grants — would lose force, removing consumer, worker, patient, and environmental protections along with compliance costs. The same void would also remove rules that structure markets, creating legal uncertainty for everyone.

industries.industry: Federal regulatory agencies and their rulemaking function
industries.note: Agencies would lose the power to issue or change any rule regulating private conduct unless Congress fully wrote the rule itself — an existential restructuring of how federal law is made. The bill does not abolish agencies but reduces them to executing statutes Congress writes in complete detail.
